vignette:
She still smells the diesel every morning when she walks into the garage—that familiar mix of grease, metal, and dust. At seventy-six, Mei-Lin’s hands are scarred and calloused from decades of turning wrenches, and she can still hear the ping of a loose bolt before anyone else can. But for the past two years, the garage hasn’t felt safe. It started with a customer—a young man who brought in a sedan with a persistent oil leak. He smiled too much, lingered too long, asked her questions about her schedule, her age, her husband. She thought nothing of it at first. She’d been a mechanic in this town for forty years; she’d seen all kinds.

Then the sedan came back to her bay again and again—brake pads, tire rotation, a mysterious rattle that never existed. He began leaving notes under the windshield wipers: “You fixed my car. Now let me fix you.” She showed them to her husband, who told her not to worry, that kids were just strange these days. But Mei-Lin noticed the sedan parked outside her shop at closing time, engine running. She noticed him standing at the back of the auto parts store when she went to buy filters. He started calling the garage line, asking for “the Asian lady who does the good work.”

The first time she saw his face in her rearview mirror—two cars behind her on the way home—her chest tightened. She took a longer route, pulled into a gas station, and watched him drive past slowly. He didn’t wave. He just stared.

Months went by. The calls and visits became more irregular, but never fully stopped. She changed her routine, switched to a different bus stop, asked her husband to pick her up. He thought she was being dramatic. She didn’t tell him about the note that appeared on her toolbox one morning, slid under the lip of the drawer: “I know where you live now.”

That was two years ago. The man was eventually arrested for stalking a different woman, and Mei-Lin thought she could breathe again. She can’t.

Now, when she works under a car, she finds herself listening for footsteps. The hydraulic lift hisses and for a split second she freezes, bracing for a hand to grab her ankle. She has stopped working late even when a job needs finishing. Her coworker, a young man named Diego, asks why she leaves so early. She just shrugs and says her joints hurt.

She still fixes cars—it’s all she knows, her father taught her before he died—but the garage no longer feels like her place. Customers who stand too close send her heart racing. A young man wearing the same style of jacket that her stalker wore makes her lose her train of thought. She once dropped a wrench because a customer laughed—a small, high laugh that reminded her of the notes.

Her husband, now retired, wonders why she jumps when he enters the kitchen quietly. She doesn’t tell him that she sleeps with the bathroom light on, or that she checks the locks three times before bed. She doesn’t tell anyone that she still sees that sedan in her mind, parked just at the edge of her vision, waiting.
